narrative:
The model estimated a 60.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means failure was judged more likely than success, and because your law school admission decision was based on this prediction, your application was rejected. This is a probability, not a certainty, but it was high enough to drive the decision.

The strongest reason was your year-three class standing: your decile of 2 was well below the average of 5.79 among accepted students, and it pushed the prediction toward failure more than any other factor. Your year-one standing was the second most influential factor; your decile of 3 was also below the accepted-student average of 6.00 and added further risk. The one major factor working in your favor was your undergraduate GPA of 3.40, which is above the accepted-student average of 3.23 and pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to outweigh the academic-standing concerns.

To improve your chances, ask admissions for specific feedback, seek academic advising, and strengthen the record that raised concern—especially your year-one and year-three performance. Consider additional coursework or retaking relevant classes, and build a structured bar-exam preparation plan. In a future application, highlight your stronger undergraduate GPA while showing concrete evidence that the earlier academic concerns have been addressed.
